flashcards.q: Why does a CNN need far fewer parameters than an MLP for the same image?
flashcards.a: Parameter sharing: a Conv2d(3->64, k=3) layer has only 3*3*3*64+64=1792 params regardless of image size, because the same kernel convolves at every position. A dense layer on a flattened 32x32x3 image to 64 units needs 196,672 params -- over 100x more.

flashcards.q: What is the CNN output-size formula, and what does 3x3/stride1/padding1 give for a 32x32 input?
flashcards.a: H' = floor((H-K+2P)/S)+1. For H=32,K=3,P=1,S=1: floor(31)+1=32 -- spatial size preserved, hence 'same' padding.

flashcards.q: What is receptive field, and how much does one 3x3 stride-1 conv layer add to it?
flashcards.a: How much of the input a feature-map location depends on. Each 3x3 stride-1 layer adds 2: RF(L)=1+2L, so 5 layers give RF=11, 10 layers give RF=21.

flashcards.q: Why is BPTT not a separate algorithm from ordinary backpropagation?
flashcards.a: Unrolling an RNN across T timesteps produces an ordinary computation graph with the same weights (W_h, W_x) reused (tied) at every step. BPTT is reverse-mode AD applied to this weight-tied graph, with the shared weight's gradient accumulated across all T timesteps -- the same rule any reused parameter gets.

flashcards.q: Why does a vanilla RNN suffer vanishing gradients across long sequences?
flashcards.a: The unrolled graph is structurally a T-layer deep network with tanh activations (derivative ceiling <1) repeated at every timestep -- the identical product-of-derivatives argument from backprop-derivation, with T (sequence length) playing the role of L (depth).

flashcards.q: Write the four LSTM gate equations.
flashcards.a: f_t=sigmoid(Wf.[h,x]+bf) forget; i_t=sigmoid(Wi.[h,x]+bi) input; g_t=tanh(Wg.[h,x]+bg) candidate; o_t=sigmoid(Wo.[h,x]+bo) output. c_t=f_t*c_{t-1}+i_t*g_t; h_t=o_t*tanh(c_t).

flashcards.q: Why does the LSTM's additive cell-state update fix vanishing gradients?
flashcards.a: d(c_t)/d(c_{t-1}) = f_t, a single learned factor per timestep the network can keep near 1, rather than a forced product of a weight Jacobian and a saturating activation derivative -- the 'constant error carousel', structurally the same idea as a residual connection's I+Jf Jacobian.

flashcards.q: Are LSTMs immune to vanishing/exploding gradients?
flashcards.a: No -- the additive cell-state path resists vanishing when the forget gate stays open, but the gates' own weight matrices and readout layers can still vanish/explode through the ordinary multiplicative mechanism. Gradient clipping remains standard practice for RNN/LSTM training regardless.

flashcards.q: Why might you still choose an LSTM over a Transformer in 2026?
flashcards.a: LSTM per-step inference cost is constant regardless of history length, unlike attention's cost growing with context length (quadratic full attention, or a growing KV cache). LSTMs can also generalize better in genuinely low-data regimes due to a stronger sequential inductive bias.

flashcards.q: Why does GlobalAveragePooling2D->Dense use far fewer parameters than Flatten->Dense, and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: GAP averages each channel over its full spatial extent, giving a C-length vector regardless of H,W, so the dense layer scales with channel count not spatial size. Tradeoff: it discards spatial position information, which matters for detection/segmentation but not whole-image classification.

flashcards.q: What is Keras 3's key architectural difference from pre-3.0 Keras, and what breaks its portability?
flashcards.a: Keras 3 is multi-backend (TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch, OpenVINO for inference), selected via KERAS_BACKEND. Using a raw backend-specific op (e.g. tf.*) instead of keras.ops.* inside a model breaks that portability.
